shorts.title: Chicago Had a 60-Mile Railroad Under Downtown
shorts.hook: Not a subway, a freight railroad.
shorts.narration_text: Not a subway, a freight railroad. Small electric locomotives hauled coal, merchandise, supplies and ash through narrow tunnels beneath the loop. The tracks connected with railroad freight houses. In some buildings, they reached directly into basement-level facilities. And this was not one tunnel linking two points. At its height, the network stretched roughly 60 miles beneath downtown Chicago. For decades, freight moved through an underground grid while the city continued above it.

shorts.title: Chicago's Freight Railroad Started as a Telephone Tunnel
shorts.hook: Chicago's underground freight railroad did not actually begin as a railroad.
shorts.narration_text: Chicago's underground freight railroad did not actually begin as a railroad. In 1899, an independent telephone company received a franchise connected to putting telephone infrastructure underground. Tunnel construction began around 1900. Those tunnels were large enough to become something more than simple cable conduits. Exactly when the freight railway idea became the real objective is not completely clear. The surviving evidence does not justify the neat story that a railroad had secretly been the plan from the first day. What is clear is the transformation. Track was installed on a two-foot gauge.

shorts.title: The Trains Stopped in 1959. The Tunnels Stayed.
shorts.hook: Then in July 1959, the trains stopped.
shorts.narration_text: Then in July 1959, the trains stopped. The railroad disappeared as a working system. The tunnels did not. So why did Chicago need an entire freight railroad beneath its streets? And how could infrastructure this extensive become obsolete? While much of its physical footprint remained, the reason begins with a problem Chicago could see every day.

shorts.title: How a Forgotten Railroad Helped Flood Downtown Chicago
shorts.hook: If a pathway still exists, something can still move through it.
shorts.narration_text: If a pathway still exists, something can still move through it. More than three decades after the last freight train ran, Chicago would get a dramatic demonstration of that fact. On April 13, 1992, water from the Chicago River began pouring into the old freight tunnel system. The breach occurred where the tunnel network passed beneath the river near the Kinsey Street area. Once the water entered, it found the legacy of the freight railroad waiting for it. A connected underground pathway through downtown. The same basic quality that had made the system valuable for freight now made it consequential for an entirely different reason.

shorts.title: The Railroad Was Closed for 33 Years. It Still Mattered.
shorts.hook: A network built to distribute freight was still physically connected enough to distribute water.
shorts.narration_text: A network built to distribute freight was still physically connected enough to distribute water. Pile driving work near the Kinsey Street bridge had taken place before the failure. And later legal claims alleged that this work had damaged or weakened the tunnel. But the legal history does not support simplifying that into a claim that a contractor was definitively found responsible for the flood. The larger point is more important to this story anyway. The freight railroad had been closed for 33 years. Its physical connectivity could still shape what happened in downtown Chicago. The flood did not bring the railroad back. It exposed something more useful for understanding cities.
